doc.title: Jimmy and Jeannie Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998

chapter: Sippie Wallace and Big Mama Thornton
title: The 'Three Generations of Blues' special with Sippie Wallace and Big Mama
summary: The KPBS special at the Belly Up Tavern, in which Sippie Wallace and Big Mama Thornton fought on stage and Jeannie sang for the first time in front of Big Mama.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Bessie, Mamie, Ma Rainey: the classic blues queens

blocks.x: Tell me about the PBS Special you did with Sippie Wallace.

And Big Mama? That was our concept. And this lady at KPBS came to us and asked if we wanted to do some kind of special or what we wanted to do. She said it would be a half hour. And so we told her what ideas we had about bringing Big Mama and Sippie Wallace and myself together — three generations of the blues. So she worked very hard, and we got this thing going. And it was the rainiest day. We were doing a jam session, still, and we set it up so that Sippie would do the first, a whole show, an hour. This was at the Belly Up.
Tavern. Which is up north in Solana Beach.
And then Big Mama would do hers. And then I would do mine. And at the end of mine we’d do a finale. But we didn’t tell Sippie or Big Mama that we were going to do a finale.
How that was going to go down.

Because they are very ornery people, both of them, and we didn’t want them to throw anything into the works. So Sippie, she did hers, and Big Mama did hers, and then when I did mine, then I said, “Ladies and Gentlemen, now we’re going to have a good old fashioned finale. And we’re going to call up these ladies, Sippie Wallace and Big Mama Thorton.” They stopped. They were at the bottom of the step watching me because they had never heard me sing. And I had played for Big Mama all these years and she had never heard me sing.
She didn’t even know she could sing.

She didn’t know I could sing, see? This was her first time. So they were standing at the bottom of the stage watching me, and so, here they come up on the stage. Now they’re going to show this young whippersnapper who— Sippie Wallace came up there and she started singing to Big Mama. And telling her off. Making up lyrics.
Oh, yeah, she was improvising.

She was improvising. And so Big Mama would take a part and then Big Mama said, [sings] “Yeah you will come to my house and I’m gonna kick you out of my back door.” “Oh no you won’t.” And I got so intrigued watching them fight, until I forgot I was supposed to sing too.
And I kind of, because I could see the cameras was on them you know. And I said, “You better get in there because it’ll never happen.”
Really. Because I forgot, I was fascinated. I was so used to playing for somebody else. And I said, “Ladies, ladies — you don’t have to fuss and fight” you know.

And when she did it, of course she had that little light growl. I mean she sliced through the whole thing. And when she did that everybody said — immediately, like lightening struck them. And they looked to her, and that’s when the camera hit her.
And so boy it was a great moment. Because they had been fighting in the dressing room.
See now if you had tried to stage that—
No way.
No way.

You know, this is one of the things that paid us off in terms of experience. Now we’d played shows of ours and all that kind of stuff, sepia clubs and all that kind of thing. So you learn that in terms of dealing with the art of improvisation, you’ve got to have a surprise.
You can’t tell them everything.
Other than that, everybody knows everything, so everybody’s going to play their hot licks or whatever, and it’s all over after that. But this way, you get the spontaneity going.
Yeah. And it’s there.
And I do the same thing with my students. They don’t know how the program is going to go until we hit.
That’s true.
They know the music you know, up to a point. But they don’t know what I’m going to do with it once we get on the stage.
